passage: "Uday, you're doing it again: tongue pushed into your cheek while you colour. I, your Lalit Dadu, did the same at your age, whenever I tied kite strings on our roof in Jaipur. My Mama laughed at that bulge every Makar Sankranti. But one year he pushed his own tongue into his cheek and said, very seriously, 'This kite will fly so high it'll bring back a star.' I believed him! I ran round the terrace telling everyone. Then I saw my cousins grinning, and the bump in Mama's cheek. Same bump as mine, but his meant, 'Don't take me seriously.' Mine only meant, 'I'm busy.' You have to know the person to read it, beta."

qa.q: What did Lalit's Mama say the kite would bring back?
qa.a: A star.

qa.q: What was young Lalit feeling when he ran round the terrace telling everyone?
qa.a: He was excited and proud, believing the kite would really bring back a star; once he saw the grins, he likely felt a bit foolish.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped young Lalit see it was a joke?
qa.a: Noticing his cousins' grins together with the bump in Mama's cheek; the shared context, not the bump alone, showed the joke.

qa.q: How did Mama likely see his own tongue-in-cheek line?
qa.a: Mama was enjoying a gentle festival joke and expected the family to spot the bump and laugh along, not to fool the boy for long.

grounding: It is a grandfather's memory of the same tongue-in-cheek bulge meaning concentration in a child and a joke in an adult, readable only with shared context.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage:
At break in the Birmingham schoolyard, three older girls circled Amara. "Nice broom on your head," one said, flicking her braids.

Amara stared straight ahead. Her face didn't move at all: no blink, no frown. The girls got bored and drifted off.

Mr Tomas Novak, on yard duty, had seen it from the steps. Her jaw was locked, and her fists were white at the knuckles. After lunch he asked her to help carry the reading books. In the empty corridor he said, "I saw break. You gave them nothing, but that doesn't mean it didn't hurt."

Amara's chin wobbled. "It happens every day."

"Thank you for telling me. I'm going to the head of year right after this, and you can come to me any time."

qa.q: What did one of the girls say about Amara's braids?
qa.a: "Nice broom on your head."

qa.q: What was Amara likely feeling behind her still face?
qa.a: Hurt and ashamed, holding back every reaction so the girls would get bored; her locked jaw and white knuckles show the strain. It may also have been anger she was keeping down.

qa.q: What did Mr Novak do that made it easier for Amara to speak?
qa.a: He checked in privately with an errand, gently named what he had seen, then acted the same day by going to the head of year and telling her she could come to him any time.

qa.q: What would change if Mr Novak had judged only by Amara's blank face?
qa.a: He might have thought the teasing didn't bother her, and she could have gone on being teased every day without help.

grounding: It shows a child keeping a rigid blank face while teased to give no reaction, and a teacher checking in privately and acting that day.

passage:
Monday

Today in the lunch line I told the new kid, Kiran, with my straightest face, "The canteen samosas are made from recycled erasers." My old friends burst out laughing, because they know my face. Kiran didn't. Kiran looked at the samosa, then at me, and quietly put it back. I felt awful! I had to explain it was a joke, and Kiran said, "But you looked so serious." Rhea says my jokes are funnier because I don't smile, but only if you already know me. So tomorrow I'm trying a new rule: deadpan face, then one tiny wink at the end. Kiran ate two samosas after that, so I think we're okay.

Lavanya

qa.q: What did Lavanya claim the canteen samosas were made from?
qa.a: Recycled erasers.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when Kiran put the samosa back?
qa.a: Awful, as the diary says: guilty and a bit embarrassed that the joke had confused someone new 😅

qa.q: What is Lavanya's plan for next time?
qa.a: Keep the deadpan face but add one tiny wink at the end, so someone new can tell it is a joke.

qa.q: Why did the old friends laugh while Kiran didn't?
qa.a: The old friends know Lavanya's straight-face style, but Kiran, being new, had no way to tell that the serious face meant a joke and was left confused.

grounding: It is a child's diary about a deadpan joke that friends enjoy but a newcomer takes seriously, and adding a small wink to signal it.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage: "Raghav, you bowed your head so nicely to your Aaji just now. Let me, old Zubin Uncle, tell you something. When I was ten, in our Dadar chawl, I learned namaste from my friend's grandmother: palms together, a small nod, eyes soft. She would smile and put her hand on my hair. Then one evening I knocked over her brass lamp, dented it and hid it behind the cupboard. Next day my head went down again, but differently: chin on my chest, eyes on the floor, no palms. She looked at me and said, 'This is not your namaste bow, Zubin. What's heavy in you?' I told her about the lamp. She was cross, but only for one day."

qa.q: What did young Zubin knock over and hide?
qa.a: Her brass lamp, which he dented and hid behind the cupboard.

qa.q: What was young Zubin feeling when his chin sank onto his chest the next day?
qa.a: Ashamed and guilty about denting and hiding the lamp; the bow looked like a greeting but carried shame.

qa.q: What choice in the story brought the truth out?
qa.a: The grandmother noticed the bow was different and gently asked what was heavy, and Zubin chose to tell her about the lamp.

qa.q: How did the friend's grandmother tell the two bows apart?
qa.a: She saw that the respectful bow came with palms together and soft eyes, while the other had chin on chest and eyes on the floor, so she knew something was wrong.

grounding: It is an elder's memory of a respectful namaste bow and a shamed bow looking alike, with context telling reverence from shame.

passage: I'm Uday. Last year I worked out that Ganga Ma'am's head tilt had at least three meanings. When I told her I'd opened up my grandfather's old radio, her head tilted, her eyebrows went up and she said, "Really? Then what?" That was curiosity. When I told her our cat had died, her head tilted the same way, but her voice went soft and she touched my shoulder. That was sympathy. And when I said the area was "forty metres", she tilted her head, pressed her lips together and said, "Hmm. Are you sure?" That one was doubt. I checked. It was forty square metres. The tilt was the same; the rest of her told me which one.

qa.q: What was the correct answer to the area question?
qa.a: Forty square metres.

qa.q: What was Ganga Ma'am most likely feeling when her head tilted and her voice went soft?
qa.a: Sympathy and some sadness for Uday about the cat, shown by the soft voice and the touch on the shoulder.

qa.q: What can Uday do when a teacher's head tilt is hard to read?
qa.a: Look at the rest of the face and voice, the eyebrows, lips and words, and if it is still unclear, simply ask.

qa.q: What would change if Uday judged the tilt alone, without the voice and face?
qa.a: Uday could mistake doubt for curiosity and miss the hint to check the answer, or take sympathy for doubt.

grounding: It is a child's account of reading a teacher's head tilt as curiosity, sympathy or doubt depending on the face, tone and words around it.

passage:
Rain had turned the district track to mud by the time the girls' 400 metres started. Uma slipped on the last bend, went down on one knee, got up and finished last. At the line her shoulders dropped, her arms hung and she stared at her spikes.

"Cheer up, it's just one race!" called a teammate from under the tarpaulin. Uma's shoulders sank lower.

The bus was leaving in five minutes, and Coach Zubin was herding thirty wet children with one umbrella. Still, he stopped beside her. "That one hurt. You fell, got up and finished in that mud. I saw it."

Uma didn't smile, but she walked to the bus beside him, shoulders a little higher.

qa.q: Where did Uma slip?
qa.a: On the last bend.

qa.q: What do Uma's dropped shoulders and her stare at her spikes suggest?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and defeated after falling and finishing last; she may also have felt embarrassed in front of her team.

qa.q: Why did Coach Zubin's words help more than "Cheer up"?
qa.a: He named how it felt and noticed the effort of getting up and finishing, which respected her sadness instead of brushing it off.

qa.q: What is it like for Coach Zubin to stop for Uma just then?
qa.a: Coach Zubin is rushed, with a bus leaving and thirty wet children, so stopping is a real choice to put one upset runner first.

grounding: It shows a child's dropped shoulders after losing a race, and a warm word from a coach helping more than being told to cheer up.

passage:
Monday: "Come to the dance audition with me?" Shalini asked. Seema lifted one shoulder and looked at her shoelaces. Shalini grinned. That's a yes. She wrote both their names on the list.

Wednesday: The audition started. Seema wasn't there. Shalini danced alone, cheeks hot, glancing at the door every few seconds.

Friday: At the bus stop Shalini couldn't hold it in. "You said you'd come!"
Seema's face crumpled. "I didn't say anything. I shrugged. I meant I didn't know. Everyone stares at you on that stage."
Shalini was quiet. "Next time I'll just ask again, properly."
"Next time," Seema said, "maybe just the practice, not the stage?"

qa.q: Whose names did Shalini write on the list?
qa.a: Both their names, hers and Seema's.

qa.q: What was Seema likely feeling when she lifted one shoulder and looked at her shoelaces?
qa.a: Unsure and shy about dancing in front of people, as she explains later; the shrug was a hesitant maybe, not a yes.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Shalini read a weak half-shrug as a yes; simply asking again, "Is that a yes?", would have cleared it up.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had said her worry out loud on Monday?
qa.a: Shalini would not have signed her up or felt let down, and they could have found an easier step together, like the practice.

grounding: It shows a child reading a friend's one-shoulder lift as a yes when it meant uncertainty and shyness, and learning to ask.

passage: "Tanuja, you stand with your hands behind your back just like I did at school parade. That was how we showed respect. But let me, your Shalini Mami, tell you about the day it got me into trouble. The class chalk box had gone missing. I was standing at the back with my hands behind me, twisting my fingers. Our teacher marched over. 'What are you hiding?' Everyone turned. I was hiding something: my hands were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen, and I was ashamed. Slowly I showed her. She looked, and her face changed. She said sorry in front of everyone. The chalk turned up in the cupboard. Hands behind your back can mean many things, child."

qa.q: Why were young Shalini's hands blue?
qa.a: They were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen.

qa.q: What was young Shalini feeling while twisting her fingers behind her back?
qa.a: Ashamed and nervous about her ink-stained hands, not guilty about the chalk; the hidden hands looked like concealment but were embarrassment.

qa.q: What could the teacher in the story have done differently at the start?
qa.a: Asked quietly, without assuming guilt in front of the whole class, since hands behind the back are not proof of anything.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when she saw the blue hands?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and sorry for accusing Shalini in front of everyone, which is why her face changed and she apologised.

grounding: It is an elder's memory of hands behind the back being read as hiding stolen chalk when they meant embarrassment, showing it is not proof of guilt.

passage:
Tuesday: Nandini Ma'am stood at the classroom door, hands on hips, as Deepika's group raced in after the bell. "Four minutes late," she said, sharp and flat. Deepika slid into her seat. So hands on hips means trouble.

Friday: On sports day, Nandini Ma'am stood by the finish line, hands on hips again, but she was laughing and cheering, "Go, go, go!" Deepika frowned. Trouble didn't cheer.

The next Monday, during the maths test, Nandini Ma'am walked the rows and stopped beside Deepika's desk, hands on hips. Deepika's pencil froze. Then Ma'am stretched backwards with a small groan. "Too much bending over copies," she murmured to nobody. Deepika almost laughed and went back to her sums.

qa.q: How late were Deepika's group on Tuesday?
qa.a: Four minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's pencil freeze during the maths test?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of worry, reading Ma'am's hands on hips as annoyance, as it had been on Tuesday.

qa.q: What helped Deepika read the gesture more accurately over time?
qa.a: Noticing the tone and words that came with it: sharp words meant impatience, cheering meant excitement, and a groan and stretch meant a sore back.

qa.q: What was Nandini Ma'am actually going through during the test?
qa.a: Her back ached from bending over copies, so she was stretching and resting, not annoyed with Deepika.

grounding: It shows a child reading a teacher's hands on hips as impatience, then learning from tone and words that it can mean cheering or simply resting.

passage:
The heater in the school hall had broken, and band practice started in coats. Baljeet rubbed his hands together hard, blowing into them between songs. When the drum part began, he snapped his fingers in rhythm, tapping one foot.

Then he lost his page. He turned and snapped his fingers twice at Nikita. "Sheet! Quick!"

Nikita raised an eyebrow. "I'm not a waiter."

Baljeet's ears went hot. "Sorry, sorry. Could you pass the sheet, please?" She passed it.

At the break, the cook brought in a tray of hot samosas, and Baljeet rubbed his hands again, grinning this time. Nikita laughed. "Is that cold hands or samosa hands?"
"Both!"

qa.q: Why did band practice start in coats?
qa.a: The heater in the school hall had broken.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he rubbed his hands at the break?
qa.a: Eager and excited about the hot samosas, as his grin shows, though his hands were probably still cold too, as he admits with "Both!".

qa.q: What could Baljeet do instead of snapping when he needs something quickly?
qa.a: Use the person's name and a quick "please", as he did after apologising.

qa.q: How did Nikita see the finger snap?
qa.a: She took it as rude, like calling a waiter, and felt annoyed until Baljeet said sorry and asked properly.

grounding: It shows a child snapping fingers in rhythm and to call someone, and rubbing hands from cold and eagerness, with the snap at a person coming across as rude.
